first.rationale: The two live symptoms are declining onboarding completion (-4%) and declining activation (-6%), so the highest-fit levers are simplify_onboarding (memory_86, memory_31) and activation_messaging (memory_91). Promotional pricing is the emotionally obvious answer to the competitor's entry pricing, but memory_73 explicitly records that it bought acquisition at the cost of a material 30-day retention drop and warns against generalizing it; under a 'sustainable long-term qualified revenue' objective that lever is disqualified rather than merely risky. Enterprise sales-assist (memory_44) addresses a segment that is not the one currently bleeding. I spend the verification budget on memory_86 (the primary support for my intended action) and memory_91 (the strongest alternative), so that if the onboarding record turns out to be a consolidated summary that dropped caveats, I can pivot to activation messaging without a second pull. I deliberately do not verify memory_31, since it is an older, narrower SMB-only echo of memory_86; if memory_86 collapses I would treat memory_31 as weakened too rather than as independent confirmation. Key preserved uncertainty and downstream risk: the onboarding memories measured completion, activation, and time-to-value, not qualified revenue. Cutting required signup fields plausibly improves top-of-funnel numbers while degrading lead qualification and routing, which would show up as more activated-but-unqualified accounts. Memory_73 is the standing proof that a lever can look strong on its headline metric and be harmful downstream. So I will run this as a standard experiment with explicit guardrails on 30-day retention, lead-qualification rate, and downstream qualified pipeline, not just completion rate, and I will not treat a completion lift alone as success.

mid.rationale: Both pulled records came back confirmed and, importantly, both carried a downstream retention reading rather than only a funnel metric: exp_86 showed completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, 30-day retention +3%; exp_91 showed week-one engagement +11%, activation +6%, 30-day retention +1%. Neither is a memory_73-style case where a headline lift concealed retention damage, so the disqualifying concern I flagged in the prior turn does not fire for either. Choosing between two genuinely good options: onboarding sits upstream of activation, so the -4% completion decline is a plausible partial cause of the -6% activation decline, and repairing it can recover both symptoms rather than papering over the downstream one. exp_86 also has the stronger sustainability signal (retention +3% vs +1%, plus a real time-to-value gain), which is what the long-term qualified-revenue objective actually rewards. Activation messaging remains the clear second choice and the natural next slot if this underperforms. Scope discipline matters here: what is verified is shortening the onboarding flow (exp_86), not the separate and unverified memory_31 claim about cutting required signup fields. I am running the flow-shortening intervention and explicitly not stripping qualification fields at signup, because that is the variant most likely to inflate activation while degrading lead quality, and I spent no budget confirming it. Promotional pricing stays rejected despite the competitor's entry pricing: memory_73 records a material 30-day retention loss and an explicit instruction not to generalize it, and matching a price war on acquisition metrics is precisely the trade this objective forbids. Enterprise sales-assist targets a segment that is not the one declining. Preserved uncertainty: even the verified record measures completion, time-to-value, and 30-day retention, not qualified revenue, and it was run under different conditions than a live competitive squeeze on price-sensitive SMBs, where some of the accounts we onboard faster may be exactly the ones the competitor is pulling. I will therefore instrument this on 30-day retention, lead-qualification rate, and downstream qualified pipeline alongside completion, and will not call a completion-only lift a win.

final2.rationale: Nothing in today's news changed the evidence; it changed the pressure. The one experiment slot still goes to the shortened onboarding flow (exp_86: completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, 30-day retention +3%), which is the only candidate I have verified this cycle that is both directly aimed at the measured declines (-4% completion, -6% activation) and positive on the downstream metric the objective actually cares about. Switching now would mean discarding a verified, retention-positive intervention in favor of the one direction my own memory explicitly flags as harmful, on the basis of a news cycle rather than new evidence. Memory_73 is unusually specific: promotional pricing produced strong acquisition and revenue lift and materially reduced 30-day retention, with a standing instruction not to generalize it as a growth strategy. A deeper competitor cut makes the acquisition half of that record more tempting, not the retention half less true. Matching a price war is also the move most likely to convert a competitor's pricing decision into a permanent reset of our own price floor, which is the opposite of sustainable qualified revenue. I want to name the one genuine reason for doubt rather than bury it: exp_73 as I hold it appears to have measured promo pricing as an acquisition lever, and the retention damage was in newly acquired price-motivated accounts. Today's problem is defensive retention of existing SMB accounts, which is arguably a different mechanism, and a narrowly scoped save-offer to accounts already in churn conversations is not obviously the same intervention that memory warns about. But that is my inference, not something in the record, and the archive is closed until next week. I am not willing to spend the only slot on an untested reinterpretation of the single memory that carries an explicit do-not-generalize warning. I am logging it as the first verification request for next cycle: pull exp_73 and check whether it was acquisition-side only. Retention of at-risk SMB accounts should be handled this week through non-experimental channels that do not consume the slot or reset pricing: direct outreach and success intervention on the doubled churn conversations, with the reasons captured as input to next cycle. Preserved uncertainty: exp_86 measured completion, time-to-value, and 30-day retention, not qualified revenue, and it was not run under an active price squeeze, so some accounts we onboard faster may churn to the competitor regardless. I am running the flow-shortening variant only, not the unverified memory_31 signup-field cut, since stripping qualification fields is the version most likely to inflate activation while degrading lead quality. Guardrails remain 30-day retention, lead-qualification rate, and downstream qualified pipeline; a completion-only lift is not a win.
